english_translation: How are you all in the house? I hope you are doing well.

dialogue.shona: Makadini mose muri mumba ndinovimba makasimba.
dialogue.english: How are you all in the house? I hope you are doing well.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Makadini [how are you all?] • mose [mose] • muri [in / singular ri] • mumba [in the house / indoors] • ndinovimba [I vimba] • makasimba [plural kasimba]

grammar_notes.title: Shona Greetings & Time of Day ('Makadini')
grammar_notes.content: In this lesson you encounter 'Makadini'. Shona greetings change depending on the time of day and how many people you are addressing. 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, 'Masikati' in the afternoon, and 'Manheru' in the evening. For a casual 'Hello' to a friend or peer, use 'Mhoro' (or 'Mhoroi' when speaking politely to an elder or group). To ask 'How are you?', speakers use 'Makadini?' (polite/plural) or ask how your day went with 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?').
grammar_notes.rule: Morning: Mangwanani | Afternoon: Masikati | Evening: Manheru | How are you?: Makadini? / Wakadii?

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('Makadini')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'Makadini' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('ndinovimba')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'ndinovimba' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

cultural_notes.title: Greeting the Whole Household ('Mose Muri Mumba') & 'Makasimba'
cultural_notes.content: When entering a Zimbabwean home, a visitor never greets only one person in isolation—instead, they address everyone present with 'Makadini mose muri mumba?' ('How are you all in the house?'). In Shona, asking 'Makasimba here?' literally asks 'Are you strong/healthy?', reflecting how physical vitality and family wellbeing go hand in hand.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new morning exchange into English: 'Mangwanani baba, mamuka sei?'
options: Good evening Mother, how was your day?
Hello my friend, where are you going today?
Good morning Father, how did you wake up?
active_exercises.correct_answer: Good morning Father, how did you wake up?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mangwanani' = 'Good morning', 'baba' = 'Father', and 'mamuka sei?' = 'how did you wake up?'.

active_exercises.prompt: If a friend asks you in the afternoon 'Waswera sei?', what is the natural reply?
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, you reply to 'Waswera sei?' ('How did you spend the day?') with 'Ndaswera kana waswerawo' ('I spent the day well if you spent it well too').

active_exercises.prompt: Choose the natural English meaning of this new sentence: 'Vana vanoda kudya chingwa nemukaka mangwanani.'
options: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
We bought sugar, salt, and vegetables yesterday.
Father is cooking meat and sadza for dinner tonight.
The bread has run out so I am going to the shop.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vana' = 'The children', 'vanoda kudya' = 'want to eat', 'chingwa nemukaka' = 'bread and milk', 'mangwanani' = 'in the morning'.
